tagline.text: A Tagbilaran harvest festival honoring Bohol's purple yam

location.label: Location
location.text: Tagbilaran City, Bohol (the venue varies, an old airport site or Plaza Rizal)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱300~1,500 (per person, food, souvenirs and transport)

children.text: The Ubi Festival is Bohol's annual purple yam (ubi) festival, with exhibits of ubi varieties from local farms, cooking contests, singing and poetry contests, and a street motorcade. The venue and dates change from year to year, so check the latest announcement before you visit.

The Ubi Festival is a local festival held every year by the Bohol provincial government's Office of the Provincial Agriculturist (OPA). Ubi is the Boholano word for purple yam, called ube in other parts of the Philippines. One Bohol tourism write-up says the event has been held since 2000, but the 2023 edition was billed as the 22nd and the 2025 edition as the 25th, so the starting year is cited differently depending on the source. The festival's aim is to honor ubi as an agricultural, historical, geographical and religious symbol and to recognize the farmers who grow it. According to one newspaper article, ubi is called a "savior crop" that eased hunger in Bohol in pre-Hispanic times.

The timing and venue change every year. The 2021 edition ran until February 24 at the old Tagbilaran airport site under COVID-19 health protocols, and the 2023 edition ran five days, from January 26 to 30, at the old city airport in Cogon, Tagbilaran. The 25th edition in 2025 ran three days, from December 3 to 5, at Plaza Rizal in Tagbilaran, a move to a more accessible spot that organizers said would bring producers closer to consumers. The dates are reported to have been moved to around December, the ubi harvest period. The 2023 edition was the first under Governor Erico Aristotle Aumentado and Vice Governor Dionisio Victor Balite, with a focus on honoring Boholano farmers and fisherfolk. Day-to-day work was reportedly handled by the OPA's Crops and Productivity Division.

The heart of the festival is the exhibit of ubi varieties. The 2023 announcement listed eight varieties: Baligonhon, Binanag, Gimnay, Binato, Iniling, Tam-isan, Kabus-ok and Kinampay. Among them, the sweet, fragrant kinampay (ubi kinampay) is the most famous and commands a premium price. The Bohol provincial government is reportedly pursuing a filing with the Intellectual Property Office of the Philippines to protect the name "ubi kinampay," and a Bohol official said, "Authentic kinampay comes from Bohol alone." Farmers reportedly plant ubi in April or May and harvest it in December. According to a 2021 report, towns such as Dauis are known for their own ubi farming, and in 2025 Dauis could not take part because its tubers were immature. This shows that the Ubi Festival is not just an event but an agricultural one that moves with the actual harvest. Organizers said they also hope it will become a place to present research and best practices.

The food is a big draw too. At a 2021 tasting, ubi jam, ubi bibingka, ubi ice cream and ubi bread were featured, along with dishes such as roasted ubi salad, ubi with crab, ubi with eggplant and cream cheese, ubi law-oy, and ubi served with fresh catch. So ubi is used as a cooking ingredient as well as a snack. Bohol is known as the country's largest ubi producer, so this is the best place to see ubi culture up close.

As of the 2023 announcement, Baligonhon, Binanag, Gimnay, Binato, Iniling, Tam-isan, Kabus-ok and Kinampay were on display. At the booths run by each local government you can compare ubi of different shapes and colors.
Sweet, fragrant kinampay is Bohol's signature variety and sells at a high price. The province's effort to protect the name was mentioned again at the 2025 edition.
In 2023 a cook-off run by the Bohol Tourism Office was held, with home cook and professional categories. In 2021, ubi bibingka, ice cream, bread and salad were featured in a tasting.

The 2023 announcement listed nine contests, including a most-participative LGU award, slogan, poetry, jingle, male and female OPM singing contests, a kuradang (traditional) contest, the cook-off and a motorcade.

On the 2023 opening day, a motorcade contest ran from the Capitol grounds to the venue at 1 p.m. After the motorcade, the opening program included the turnover of ubi planting materials and the opening of the exhibits.
On the last day, contest winners and participating towns are honored. In 2023 an awards program for outstanding Boholano farmers was also held, reported to cover 22 categories.
In 2025, 19 towns took part in the exhibits. Organizers said they hope the event will connect producers and consumers.

blocks.title: A theme that changes every year

children.text: The 2021 theme, in Boholano, expressed the idea of overcoming hunger caused by COVID-19 with ubi, and the 2025 theme was "Ubi' ng Bol-anon: Tinubdan sa Pagkaon, Garbo sa Kulturang Bol-anon" (The Boholano Ubi: Source of Food, Pride of Boholano Culture). The festival treats ubi not just as a crop but as part of Bohol's identity.
Arrive at the venue and tour the town booths to see the ubi varieties. The venue changes every year, so check the announcement before you arrive.
Taste snacks and dishes made with ubi. Ubi jam, bread and ice cream are typical souvenirs.
Have lunch at a nearby restaurant and rest.
Watch any contest of the day, such as singing or the cook-off. The program differs from day to day.
The program differs by year and by day. Check the official schedule in announcements from the Bohol Tourism Office and the provincial agriculture office.

items.title: Tagbilaran day plan
items.subtitle: The festival and the city sights

children.text: Have breakfast in Tagbilaran and head to the festival grounds.
Enjoy the exhibits and tastings.
In the afternoon, look around Tagbilaran. See the Tagbilaran entry for a detailed route.
Return to your lodging around sunset.

On January 26 at 1 p.m., a motorcade contest ran from the Capitol grounds to the venue, followed by the opening program. The opening program included speeches, the turnover of ubi planting materials and fruit seedlings, the turnover of an RPC to the farmers' organization PIWARDEP, and the ribbon cutting for the exhibits.
On the second day, town booths with ubi displays were set up at the venue and contest participation began.
On the third day the cook-off run by the Bohol Tourism Office was held, together with product sampling from the distillery Destileria Barako.
On January 30, contest winners and participating towns were recognized in a program led by the governor.
This schedule is an example based on the 2023 announcement. Programs differ every year, so check the latest notice.

Fly from Manila to Bohol-Panglao International Airport (TAG). The airport is on Panglao Island, and you reach central Tagbilaran by taxi or van over land. Travel time and fares vary with the season and traffic, so confirm locally.
You can also take a ferry from Cebu to Tagbilaran port. Schedules and fares differ by operator, so check before you book.
Within the city, tricycles and jeepneys are the usual choice. The venue changes every year between the old airport site in Cogon and Plaza Rizal, so confirm the location before you arrive.
The area around the venue can be crowded, so walking or a tricycle is easier.

The festival has often been held between December and January, right after the ubi harvest. One farmer said ubi is planted in April or May and harvested in December, and the 2025 edition was held in early December. But the 2021 edition ran until February 24 and the 2023 edition ran January 26–30, so it varies by year.
Bohol's dry season generally runs from December to May. If the festival falls in that period, it is a good time for the outdoor exhibits.

One blog says the festival is held every January 27, but that does not match recent records (February 2021, January 26–30, 2023, and December 3–5, 2025). Do not treat the date as fixed, and check the announcement every year.

Tagbilaran is Bohol's central city and has a range of hotels and guesthouses. Lodging in town can fill up during the festival, so book ahead. You can also stay at a beach on Panglao Island and travel to Tagbilaran.

Ubi products are the core of the food. Try ubi jam, bibingka, ice cream and bread, and dishes such as roasted ubi salad or ubi served with crab, which you can find at the festival. At other times, look for ubi desserts at local Bohol restaurants.

The dates and venue change every year. Check the latest announcements from the Bohol Tourism Office or the provincial agriculture office first. The 2021 edition was at the old airport site, the 2023 edition at the old city airport in Cogon and the 2025 edition at Plaza Rizal.
Buy ubi products directly at the booths. Compare prices locally.
The venue is often outdoors. Bring a hat, sunscreen and water.
The contest schedule (cook-off, singing contests) differs by day, so get the timetable in advance if you want to see a particular one.
Traffic in Tagbilaran can be heavy during the festival, so allow extra travel time.
Bring plenty of cash. Small booths may not take cards.
Check for allergies and dietary restrictions before eating ubi.
The festival schedule changes every year and may be canceled or postponed, so check announcements before you travel.
Health protocols may apply in circumstances such as COVID-19.
It is a crowded event, so watch out for pickpockets.
It is an outdoor event, so be ready for midday heat and sudden rain.
Some towns may not take part depending on the harvest. In 2025, Tagbilaran and Dauis did not participate.
Check expiry dates and packaging on processed products.
